24.0.0.en: If a man discovers a defect in the woman he has taken as a wife, a physical defect or one of conduct, which he sees as an obstacle to continuing a happy life with her, the divorce must not be verbal, but he must write a bill of divorce, give it to her, and send her out of his house.

24.0.1.en: Although God does not love divorce, He allowed it for the following reasons:

24.0.2.en: 1- The man who hates his wife humiliates her and is harsh to her, so divorce is a liberation for her from this harshness, which the man at that time could have inflicted on her.

24.0.3.en: 2- Writing a bill of divorce, which is done in the presence of accredited witnesses, gives the man an opportunity to reconsider if he was hasty in his decision.

24.0.4.en: 3- The man who divorced his wife is not permitted to take her back if she has married another (v. 4), so that the man would not rush into hating his wife or divorcing her.

24.0.5.en: This law protects against the evil customs that the Egyptians had anciently, which was the exchange of wives if the men felt hatred for their wives.

24.1.0.en: If the divorced woman married another man and then the latter divorced her and gave her a bill of divorce, or died, she may not return to her first husband. This is considered an abomination, because the first husband considers his wife to have been defiled by living with another man, so he hates her more than before, and even if he shows willingness for her to return, he goes back to treating her badly. Therefore God forbade this kind of marriage, since it is considered a sin that defiles the Promised Land, which God purified by driving the pagans out of it so that His people might dwell in it.

24.2.0.en: Charged with any business ("a charge laid upon him"): any work for the benefit of the people is required of him.

24.2.1.en: This commandment shows God's concern for marriage, for it exempts one who marries for a year from taking part in the war and from all the works required for the community, for the following reasons:

24.2.2.en: 1- So that he may have an opportunity for marital understanding and for adapting with his bride to the new life and forming good habits by which the two will live throughout their lives.

24.2.3.en: 2- He has an opportunity to express his love and make his wife happy during this year, so that their good relationship is established and they rejoice all their lives.

24.2.4.en: 3- So that the man will not be anxious about his bride during the war and so fail to attend to the responsibilities of war.

24.2.5.en: 4- The man may be exposed to death in the war, and this would be very hard for his bride, who did not enjoy her marriage even for a year.

24.2.6.en: God's purpose in your marriage and in your being among people is that you form relationships with them that make them glad and make their lives happy. So try to express your love for those around you with words, smiles, gifts, or gentle touches by which you make them feel your love, and so you will strengthen your family relationships and gladden their hearts.

24.3.0.en: The mill: a tool for grinding grain consisting of two stones, an upper and a lower. The upper one moves and the lower one is fixed.

24.3.1.en: The upper millstone: the upper stone of the mill.

24.3.2.en: The Law forbids taking the whole mill, or one of its two stones, as a pledge for a debt. For the mill is the tool with which the grain from which bread is made is ground, so taking it means depriving its owner of his basic food and thus exposing his life to hunger and death.

24.4.0.en: Makes merchandise of him ("enslaves him"): from servitude, that is, makes him his slave.

24.4.1.en: If a Jew is found who is so hard-hearted that he steals one of his brothers to make him his slave or to sell him as a slave to others, this man must be put to death to remove the sin of harshness and theft, which in this case reaches the level of the sin of murder, because he has taken away a human being's life.

24.4.2.en: Do not hurt a person's feelings with wounding words, even if it is in reply to a wrong from him, for this is considered a moral killing, an insult, and the taking away of his rights as a human being accepted in society. Be tender, and you will enjoy the tenderness of God.

24.5.0.en: The Lord warns them of the necessity of applying the law of leprosy and of acting with all exactness on the instructions of the priests which the Lord taught them. (The details of the law of leprosy are given in Lev 13, 14.)

24.6.0.en: He reminds them of what happened to Miriam, the sister of Moses, when she and Aaron murmured against him after their departure from Egypt, that is, in the wilderness of Sinai, because he was alone in leadership, and God struck her with leprosy (Num 12) and they put her outside the camp in application of the law of leprosy. Miriam was not excepted because she was a prophetess or because she was the sister of Moses, and therefore the law of leprosy must be applied to all the people with all exactness.

24.6.1.en: Keep away from everything that defiles your thoughts and your senses, because you are a man of God, and so you will live pure and be able to feel God in your life, and He will bless you.

24.7.0.en: The purpose of this legislation is to preserve the dignity of the poor man if he borrows money from another person. It is not permitted for that other person to break into the poor man's house to take a pledge, because of the insult and humiliation this carries for the poor man; rather, the lender must stand outside the house so that the owner of the house may bring the pledged item out to him, and so that the creditor does not wrong the poor man and take from his house something more than the pledge. Justice must be applied however poor or weak the person is, because the creditor may become covetous when he sees the contents of the poor man's house and demand the pledge of many belongings in payment of his debt, or may go back on lending to him, demanding that he sell what he has and meet his needs.

24.8.0.en: If a person needs money and is compelled to pledge his garment, and if he cannot repay the money within that day, the creditor is bound to return his garment to him, because it is his essential need to cover his body while he sleeps.

24.9.1.en: The Lord commands that the hired servant who works for another for wages not be wronged, especially if he is poor, whether he is an Israelite or one of the strangers dwelling in the various cities of Israel.

24.10.0.en: Do not delay giving him his wages for which he worked, day by day, for he needs them and has exhausted himself the whole day to earn them. For if he feels wronged by the one he worked for, he will complain of him to the Lord, and the Lord will judge the wrongdoer and punish him for his injustice.

24.11.0.en: This law makes clear each person's responsibility for his own sin, so a judge is not to sentence a father to death because of his son's sin, nor a son because of his father's sin, as He affirmed in (Ezek 18:4). But the visiting of the iniquity of the fathers upon the children (Ex 20:5) means the spread of sin from the fathers to the children, who learn it from their fathers, so God repays the fathers and the children, each for his own sin. But if the children refuse to continue in the sin of their fathers, God will not punish them.

24.11.1.en: Be just in your judgments; do not be swayed by sweet words, and do not favor the rich and the strong, or a relative or a friend, but hold to the truth for the sake of God, who stands before you, and He will protect you from many injustices, and will be just with you, and will reward you for all your good works with eternal life.

24.12.0.en: The Lord demands justice in judgments, so the stranger is not to be wronged because he is not of the children of Israel, nor the orphan, because he has no one to defend him or claim his right.

24.12.1.en: Likewise, it is not right to take as a pledge the garment of a widow, which is her covering and her protection from cold and heat (as mentioned in v. 13); rather, lending to her is to please the Lord and a generosity on the part of the lender.

24.13.0.en: He reminds them of the bitterness of exile and need when they were enslaved in the land of Egypt and nothing delivered them from it except the intervention of the Lord who redeemed them. So as they experienced misery and suffering, they can appreciate the need of the wretched for mercy and compassion, and hasten to rescue them from their misery. He therefore commands them that, as He did with them and rescued them, they also should do the same with these.

24.14.0.en: In this verse and the following verses to the end of the chapter, the Lord teaches them the principles of works of mercy toward the poor. In this verse the Lord commands them that when they harvest their fields, if they forget a sheaf of the harvest in the field and remember it, they are not to go back to get it, but leave it for those who need it among the strangers, orphans, and widows who go out into the fields to gather what remains after the harvest for their necessary food. If they do this, the Lord will bless all their works and increase their good things, as He said in (Lev 19:9, 10, 2 Cor 9:6).

24.15.0.en: The method followed for harvesting olives was that the fruit of the olive branches was made to fall to the ground by means of long sticks. Here too the Lord commands them that the berries that may remain on the branches are not to be gone back for, but are also left for the same needy groups mentioned above.

24.16.0.en: You shall glean it ("go over the boughs again"): you pick up the leavings of the picking.

24.16.1.en: The same applies to the gathering of clusters of grapes from the vineyard. Do not go back again to pick what remains on the vine of the grapes, but leave it as a portion for the needy groups.

24.17.0.en: He encourages them in the previous works of mercy by recalling the feelings of humiliation and poverty that they suffered in the days of bondage in Egypt, so that they may hasten to have compassion on the needy.

24.17.1.en: Justice, penalties, and the brother's widow

25.0.0.en: God calls the judges to justice in acquitting the righteous and punishing the guilty when they are asked to judge in any quarrel or dispute.

25.1.0.en: He tells us about the punishment of the guilty by beating or flogging them, and he stipulates the following for it:

25.1.1.en: 1- The flogging is to be done before the judge, so that he may be sure that it is carried out in the amount that he sentenced.

25.1.2.en: 2- The stripes are not to exceed 40 stripes, lest the guilty man feel more humiliation and contempt than he can bear, and so that he does not faint physically or die.

25.1.3.en: It appears here that the purpose of the punishment is discipline and not humiliation. Christ was struck 39 stripes, and if we add the crown of thorns and the spear the number becomes 41; this is what the Church cries out in every prayer, saying "Lord, have mercy" 41 times, because Christ bore these sufferings on account of our sins.

25.1.4.en: If you are in charge and order discipline for a child or an adult, let it be within the limits of what benefits him and not what breaks him psychologically or physically. And may you convince him of the reason for the punishment, even if he is a child, and do not forget to show him also your love and your mercy.

25.2.0.en: It was the custom among the pagan peoples to put a muzzle on the mouth of the ox when it pulled the threshing sledge to thresh the various grains. But God's mercy appears in that He commands His people to let the ox eat the straw it needs so that it can continue its work. The meaning of this is kindness to animals, and all the more to man, so everyone who toils in a work should be rewarded, especially if it is the service of God, as is made clear in (1 Cor 9:9).

25.2.1.en: Take care to reward everyone who toils in any work, whether done for you or in the service of God, even if only with encouraging words, concern, and care, and if he is in need, attend to his material needs.

25.3.s.en: (3) The law of marriage to the wife of the deceased

25.3.0.en: If a man dies and leaves his wife without having had a child by her, his brother is bound to marry her to raise up offspring, whose firstborn is counted as belonging to his dead brother. The brothers often lived together in one large dwelling, each with his family, as still happens in some villages. The new husband is responsible for his brother's widow, who has become his new wife, and takes care of all her needs, and it is not right for the wife to marry anyone other than her husband's brother unless this brother refuses.

25.4.0.en: If the husband's brother refuses to marry his brother's widow, as happened with the sons of Judah (Gen 38:8), and this shows that this custom was ancient, before the Law of Moses, the Law stipulates, to establish this heinous fault against the refusing brother, who fails to bear the responsibility and to preserve his brother's right to the inheritance of the Promised Land, which symbolizes the Kingdom of Heaven, that the widow of the dead man go to the elders of the city, who gather in the square at the gate of the city, and declare to them that her husband's brother refuses to bear the responsibility and to raise up offspring for his brother.

25.5.0.en: The elders try to persuade this brother to bear his responsibility and marry his brother's widow, and if he persists in refusing, the elders establish this against him by his plain confession; then, in contempt of this heinous conduct, the widow takes off this man's sandal and gives it to the elders as a testimony to his refusal to bear responsibility and a declaration that it is not permitted for him to walk on his brother's land, that is, his inheritance; and the widow spits in his face as a declaration of the contempt of the whole people for him, and they call his name all his life "The house of him that hath his shoe loosed," that is, the house of the one who refuses to bear his responsibility and who violates the Law.

25.5.1.en: After the brother's refusal to marry his brother's widow, they look for the nearest relative of the dead man, who is called the kinsman, as happened with Boaz and Ruth (Ruth 4), and if all refuse, the Law permits the wife to marry whom she wishes. Therefore in the Church of the New Testament the priest and the deacons take off their shoes on entering the sanctuary as a declaration that they are not the ones responsible for the salvation of people, but Christ alone is the Savior and they are only His servants. So too does every person at Communion, as a declaration of his weakness and his need of Christ his Savior.

25.5.2.en: Do not be negligent in your responsibilities, for you are a steward over them before God, and He will hold you to account for them on the Day of Judgment; and if you feel your inability, ask for His help, and He will not forsake you, and you will rejoice in experiencing His work in you.

25.6.s.en: (4) The woman and the quarrel of men

25.6.0.en: His secrets ("his nakedness"): his reproductive organs.

25.6.1.en: If two men get into a fight because of a dispute or quarrel between them, and the wife of one of them comes and intervenes in the fight in order to rescue or support her husband against the other man, and she commits a shameful act showing impudence and recklessness, and even a desire to kill him, in that she seizes his private parts to force him to let go of her husband, the commandment here orders that this wife's hand be cut off, because by this she has cast off modesty and dignity and lost shame. Leaving her without punishment could cause others to stumble and encourage other women to do that act; therefore she is not to be treated with pity, but is to be an example to the others.

25.6.2.en: Do not be harsh in your dealings with people even if one of them provokes you and is insolent toward you, for self-defense does not mean revenge and an attempt to destroy the other.

25.7.0.en: God forbids cheating in weights and measures. The merchants used to carry the various weights in a bag in which they moved about, while the measures they kept in their houses. So it is not right for the merchant to have two weights, buying with the large and selling with the small, and likewise in measures (Lev 19:35, 36, Prov 11:1).

25.8.0.en: The Lord commands that one weight or measure be used for selling and buying, which is just and true, without cheating, for cheating in weights and measures is lying and stealing. If a person is honest in his dealings, the Lord makes his life on earth happy and blessed and gives him offspring who live always on the holy land. But cheating is an abomination to the Lord, and the curse falls on the one who commits it as a recompense for his deceit toward others.

25.8.1.en: Be honest in your dealings with others even if you have an opportunity to deceive them, and do not justify cheating by saying that you are in need and they are rich, or that they are thieves and so it is permissible to steal from them.

25.9.0.en: Amalek: a people descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob.

25.9.1.en: The Lord reminds them of the hostility that Amalek showed when they met the children of Israel on their departure from Egypt on their way to the Promised Land.

25.10.0.en: Amalek attacked the elders and the children who were weary from journeying from place to place in Sinai, who were slow in walking and lagged behind the group, and Amalek took advantage of their being separated from the rest, taking some of them captive and killing others. This act of theirs was evidence of their wickedness and of the absence of the fear of God in their hearts. Had they been honorable warriors, they would have come forward to confront and fought the strong of the people, and not the sick and the weak (Ex 17:8).

25.11.0.en: The Lord commands them here that, when they are settled in the land He gives them and have rest from the labors of travel and the wars with their enemies around them, they are to destroy the Amalekites and remove any trace of them from the face of the earth, so that they may never rise again.

25.11.1.en: The Lord warns them against forgetting to carry out this command, because the continued existence of Amalek constitutes a permanent danger to their peace, and this was done in many stages, as in (Num 14:45, Judg 3:12-20, Judg 6:3, 33, 1 Sam 27:8, Job 4:14, Isa 3:1-9) until they perished completely, so that they no longer exist now.

25.11.2.en: Injustice is always temporary, and the time will come when the injustice falls as punishment on the head of the wrongdoer. So do not persist in taking away the rights of others by not giving them an opportunity to defend themselves, or ridiculing their words, or using your authority in any way to restrict their freedom.
